song.title: As The Sun Rises
song.author: Mark and Helen Johnson
song.summary: A song of faith and gratitude to welcome any new day with hope and positivity. Focusing on the goodness of God, and our daily response to His love, this is a song of praise for any assembly. With fabulous harmonies and a contagious chorus, this is a song to lift our spirits. ‘As the sun rises on a new day, may our hearts say, “God is good to us”.’
song.teachingTips:
• In your warm-up, focus on breathing to help sustain the lyrical melody in this song.
  • The choruses should be positive and punchy, sung with lots of energy. Be sure to separate and emphasize important lyrics such as ‘God is good to us’ so they can be heard. Contrast this in the verses with a legato sound and use good breath control to make sure the long C (on ‘change’ in verse 1) is held for its full four beats.
  • As the melody goes quite low in the register in the chorus (on ‘You are faithful God’/‘We are grateful Lord’), be careful not to let these words die away too much – good breath support is important here.

assembly.title: Super Seeds
assembly.description: This assembly encourages us to look at the potential of seeds for new life and growth and also provides an opportunity to explore our own potential.

assembly.title: Light and Colour
assembly.description: This assembly encourages us to open our eyes to the colours of springtime, talking about our favourite colours, noticing the extra daylight and appreciating nature's use of colour and light.

assembly.title: Extra Energy
assembly.description: What wakes you up in the morning? From birdsong to sprouting leaves and Easter eggs, this assembly helps us to celebrate all the energy of springtime.

assembly.title: Turning Over a New Leaf
assembly.description: This assembly looks at new leaves and growth in nature and helps us all to look within ourselves to see where we might want to ‘turn over a new leaf’ too.

assembly.title: People Who Care
assembly.description: The ideal assembly to help us to focus on, appreciate and celebrate all those who help and care for us.

assembly.title: The World Around
assembly.description: From the tallest trees, to the something you can only see with a microscope, this assembly encourages us to notice, appreciate and be thankful for the world around us.

assembly.title: It’s Challenging
assembly.description: By looking at changes in nature, this assembly helps us to explore change and how it can sometimes be difficult.

assembly.title: Happy Endings
assembly.description: This assembly explores setbacks we might encounter in our lives and the characteristics needed to overcome them.

assembly.title: Feeling Hopeful
assembly.description: This assembly explores the meaning of hope and what it will take to realize our ambitions for the future.

assembly.title: Feeling Awake
assembly.description: This assembly uses The Parable of the Sower to reflect on what is needed to be ‘awake and ready for action’ in school.

assembly.title: Feeling Good
assembly.description: This assembly explores the uniqueness of human beings and how we can help others to feel more valuable.

assembly.title: Good Or Sad Friday?
assembly.description: This assembly explores the emotions of happiness and sadness and reflects on whether Easter is a sad or happy time for Christians.

assembly.title: Easter Message
assembly.description: This assembly uses the idea of code-breaking to help consider the special message of Easter.

resources.title: Composing Over A Drone
resources.content:
[{"key":"d0c8b69c2f8763ed","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To compose a short pentatonic melody above a drone
  • To begin to use standard notation to record a composition
  • To sing a song with harmony parts. 
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"b1601dc03c53fafd","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Amplified sound system; tuned instruments e.g. glockenspiels (pre-prepared to include only the notes C D E G A); note cards or black/white board 

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"50ca000b555e64da","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

If you listen really carefully to the chorus you might notice that it mainly has the same bass note in the piano – B♭ – and only briefly strays to other nearby notes. This is called a tonic (the first note of the scale), pedal note or root note and reinforces the key of the song (B♭ major). It can often be used as a drone which plays continuously beneath a melody. Using pitched percussion instruments or keyboards and working in pairs, ask the class to compose their own simple melodies over a drone in the bass.

To do this, use a pentatonic scale starting on C. Give the children the notes C D E G A to choose from (write the note names and standard notation on cards or on the board) and remind them to use short and long notes. 

","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"e1ee905d203397be","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicActivities/musicactivities-composing-over-a-drone-1616584467vBS9w.png","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"65b1b7cc5fc8df42","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

It will sound best if the melody starts and finishes on C (the tonic of this scale). One pupil plays the melody while their partner plays the C drone. Then swap over. 

","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"62919f34a55197f3","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Using the letter names, see if the children can write out their melodies on strips of paper. Encourage them to add other details like tempo – is it fast, slow or something in between? Write this at the beginning of the ‘score’ – and dynamics (ff, f, F, P, p, pp). Some children might be able to try using standard music notation to write out the notes of their melodies. 

","title":"Step It Up!","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/u1873-1614695091mFFrP.png"}},{"key":"6054ac72105dbdfb","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Drones are used in all genres of music, including medieval, classical, popular and folk music. Try listening to the opening of John Adams’s Shaker Loops 1 or some Scottish bagpipe music, in which a low drone is always clearly heard. 

","title":"Listen","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/listen-01-1615991956LRT6z.png"}},{"key":"6ec4e3c8e73b7ff9","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lpZiPZwwXhM","title":"Amazing Grace on the bagpipes","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}}]
resources.summary: Investigate the use of drones/pedal notes in music and work with a partner to compose a simple melody to play over the top of a drone.

resources.title: Revelations Dance
resources.content:
[{"key":"7993e3f2ab83b89a","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

This is a useful and informative dance to watch around Easter <\/strong>time. Alvin Ailey (1960) created this three-part dance about African-American history, which depicts the struggle from slavery to freedom. Its story can be interpreted to be more generally about struggle and conflict within oneself, but how holding on to faith<\/strong> can pull you through. The Take Me To The Water <\/em>baptism scene is a good reference when thinking about Easter: the dancers perform as if they are being ‘reborn’, fitting the story of the resurrection. The final section is performed as the dancers rejoice in church. <\/p>\n","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"ef1cba01667bc607","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https:\/\/www.youtube.com\/watch?v=RrPJ4kt3a64","title":"Alvin Ailey's Revelations","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"af267592355beab9","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"","title":"The dancers discuss what the dance means to them","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}}]

resources.title: Composition Wheels
resources.content:
[{"key":"bc73fc2fd761bc87","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Ideal for 2 sessions

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"8cb4e0c157348b35","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To recognize different instrumental timbres and their effects
  • To combine several layers of sound and describe the effect
  • To create and follow a graphic score
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"e59388d2409e6c52","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Large sheets of paper; pens; card; split pins; tuned and untuned percussion instruments

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"174544d6ec695e53","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Dynamics; forte; loud/strong; piano; soft; tempo; fast; slow; timbre; texture; musical layers; conductor; graphic score 

","title":"Key vocabulary","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/icons-keyvocab-280x280-27-1620218359Ng3ET.png"}},{"key":"44f524b885f25e5e","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

The songs chosen for this activity are based on the theme of ‘morning’.  

Arrange the class into groups and provide a large sheet of paper and pens for each group.  

Listen to Sun Arise and ask the class to draw images inspired by the song. As well as visual ideas such as sun, trees etc., encourage the class to think about different sounds, colours and moods that come to mind as they listen.  

Next, provide a selection of instruments for each group and ask them to think about different ways to represent the ideas on their paper using their instruments, and vocal and body sounds (e.g. whistling for birds singing, shakers for rustling trees, a cymbal played with a soft beater to represent warmth, chimes for the blowing breeze).

Encourage the group to think about varying musical dimensions such as dynamics or tempo to achieve the different effects.

Once the children have collected a range of different sounds, assign a different abstract symbol to each, e.g.  

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"97d5762d2fef9738","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/year3/year3-musiccurr-compositionwheels-1635426932mDdX7.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"387ffb5cf078855a","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Composition Wheels 

Next, draw three concentric circles on a piece of card and plot the symbols in different parts of the circle. Then, create a pointer and attach it to the centre of the card using a split pin. Create one wheel for each group. One member of the group takes the role of ‘conductor’ and spins the pointer, while the other members of the group play the corresponding sounds. Discuss how the texture changes at every spin as more sounds are added or taken away. Explain that this is a form of graphic score.  

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"cf83582859a81d64","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/year3/year3-musiccurr-compositionwheels2-1635426933CyeXk.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"850dec424281d2b2","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Try using the Composition Wheels as an introduction to a performance of Sun Arise.  

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"a27da1f2af37162a","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Create a whole-class composition by asking each of the groups to perform their composition wheels together. One member of each group should spin the pointer to change the musical texture, and a signal to end the music should be agreed.  

","title":"Step It Up!","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/u1873-1614695091mFFrP.png"}},{"key":"5433285c2ede912f","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/year3/year3-musiccurr-compositionwheels3-16354269341DcpD.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"ff9c021619cd6887","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Challenge the children to create their own Composition Wheels based on a chosen theme (e.g. space, the Great Fire of London, rainforests, rivers). 

","title":"Branch Out","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/u1874-1614695090s5QJx.png"}},{"key":"68960506c7b26305","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

How have other composers interpreted the theme of morning? Listen to ‘Morning Mood’ from Peer Gynt Suite No. 1  by Edvard Grieg, or use one of the song choices and get the children to draw what they hear. 

","title":"Listen","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/listen-01-1615991956LRT6z.png"}},{"key":"c039191895b47b7c","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":" https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J-1Bob1dU18","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"e41f4e742da6de03","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"Assessment Suggestions","background_color":"#009CCF"}},{"key":"83996eec1eadc143","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"
  • Can they respond imaginatively to music, describing the ideas and images it evokes? 
  • Can they investigate different ways of using voices, body percussion and instruments to achieve an effect? 
  • Can they create and follow graphic notation? 
  • Can they give performance directions (e.g. taking the role of conductor)?
","title":"","noMargin":false}}]

resources.title: Drones And Melodies
resources.content:
[{"key":"ee16c503146dfbab","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Ideal for 1-2 sessions

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"be512574055be57a","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To compose a short pentatonic melody above a drone
  • To notate a melody using staff and letter notation
  • To sing a song with harmony parts
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"85f427eff15b606f","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Tuned instruments (glockenspiels, xylophones, boomwhackers); paper and pens; manuscript paper

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"fc37c62cffdd3ecd","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Pentatonic; melody; bass note; tonic; pedal note; root note; drone; largo; andante; allegro; mezzo forte; forte; fortissimo; pianissimo; piano; mezzo piano; bagpipe; chanter; homophonic; texture

","title":"Key vocabulary","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/icons-keyvocab-280x280-27-1620218359Ng3ET.png"}},{"key":"b2126dfd9009f3c9","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

If you listen really carefully to the chorus of As The Sun Rises, you might notice that it mainly has the same bass note in the piano (B) and only briefly strays to other nearby notes. The first note of a scale is called the tonic, pedal note or root note and reinforces the key of the song (B major in this case).

Using pitched percussion instruments or keyboards and working in pairs, ask the class to compose their own simple melodies over a drone in the bass. To do this, use a major pentatonic scale starting on C. Give the children the notes C D E G A to choose from (you could write the note names or display standard notation).

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"0aa151b02a00a004","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/YEAR5/year5-musiccurr-dronesandmelodies-excerpts-v22-1640018098TIYnl.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"1f701033769bf088","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Explain that it will sound best if the melody starts and finishes on C (the tonic). One child plays the melody while their partner plays the C drone. Then, swap over.

Using the letter names, see if the children can write out their melodies on strips of paper, selecting the order of pitches they intend to use. Encourage them to add other details like tempo markings – is it fast (allegro), slow (largo) or something in-between (andante)? Write this at the beginning of the score and add some dynamics (pianissimo (), piano (), mezzo piano (), mezzo forte (), forte (), fortissimo ()).

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"1129b532af5b524d","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/YEAR5/year5-musiccurr-dronesandmelodies-v2-16400112825MO6r.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"d68f9cb7b5a5ca2e","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/YEAR5/year5-musiccurr-dronesandmelodies-excerpts-v2-1640018098q3WBL.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"bda35ece288bc798","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Homophonic texture in music occurs when a single line of melody is accompanied by harmonic parts. In Scottish bagpipe music, for example, the single bagpipe plays a melody and this is accompanied by a drone.

Listen to these traditional tunes, Amazing Grace and The Peacock Followed The Hen, played on the bagpipes. The children should be able to hear the low drone acting as an accompaniment to the main melody.

","title":"Listen","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/listen-01-1615991956LRT6z.png"}},{"key":"b7aa54d1c22b5496","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lpZiPZwwXhM","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"c560477d7a317481","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lBPBJNAR2wM","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"ccd6e05d2d9babe1","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Discuss how instrumental timbres and styles of music can reflect and communicate the national identity of a country. Explain that the bagpipe is a wind instrument and is the national instrument of Scotland. It is made up of a number of pipes and a bag. The pipe that plays the melody is known as a chanter and the piper covers the finger holes to create the tune. The other pipes are called drones because they produce single notes. The piper blows into the pipe that fills the bag and the air pressure allows the reeds to vibrate in the chanter and drones so that the melody and drones can be played at the same time. To take a breath, the piper squeezes the bag and this keeps the bagpipe playing its continuous sound.

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"e275274770bc3340","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"ASSESSMENT SUGGESTIONS","background_color":"#009CCF"}},{"key":"04362591666cce30","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"
  • Can they improvise melodies over a drone?
  • Can they compose and notate a pentatonic melody using staff or letter notation?
  • Can they add simple performance directions (e.g. dynamics, tempo) to their compositions?
  • Can they recognize specific features of the music they listen to (e.g. the use of drones)?
","title":"","noMargin":false}}]
